content: 1. Visitors and accompanying persons should be provided with clear instructions on how to minimize the risk of infection transmission in healthcare settings. 2. Healthcare workers (HCWs) responsible for collecting specimens from patients with acute respiratory diseases (ARDs) must wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) as specified, including the use of biohazard specimen bags with proper labeling and accompanying request forms. 3. Personnel involved in the transport of specimens should be trained in safe handling practices and spill decontamination procedures to ensure safety. 4. Laboratories within healthcare facilities (HCFs) must adhere to biosafety protocols appropriate to the organisms being handled. 5. All specimens should ideally be delivered by hand, avoiding the use of pneumatic tube systems for transport. The accompanying request form must clearly indicate suspected ARD of potential concern, and the laboratory should be notified in advance of the specimen's arrival. 6. All clinical specimens should be treated as potentially infectious, and HCWs handling or transporting them must strictly follow infection control precautions to minimize exposure to pathogens. 7. HCF administrators should ensure HCWs are immunized against seasonal influenza whenever possible and monitor vaccine uptake. WHO guidelines for seasonal influenza vaccination are available online. 8. HCWs at higher risk (e.g., pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, or those with cardiopulmonary conditions) should be informed of their medical risks and offered alternative work assignments that do not involve direct care for ARD patients. 9. HCFs managing patients with ARDs of potential concern should maintain a register of HCWs who have provided care for these patients for contact tracing purposes. 10. A surveillance system for influenza-like illness (ILI) among HCWs should be developed, particularly for those caring for ARD patients, with self-reporting of symptoms encouraged. 11. HCWs should have prompt access to diagnostic services, counseling, and treatment if available. If antiviral prophylaxis is recommended, systems should be in place to provide it to exposed HCWs. 12. HCF administrators should ensure timely access to newly developed vaccines for HCWs caring for ARD patients and provide additional emotional and family support as needed. 13. HCWs should monitor themselves for ILI symptoms (e.g., cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing) for 7–10 days after their last exposure to an ARD patient. If symptoms develop, they should immediately isolate themselves, notify infection control teams, and avoid public areas. 14. Patients with ARDs caused by novel organisms with high public health impact should be placed in airborne precaution rooms with adequate ventilation (≥12 air changes per hour). If such rooms are unavailable, single rooms with proper ventilation should be used. 15. Triage and waiting areas should be well-ventilated (≥12 air changes per hour) and organized to maintain at least 1-meter distance between patients. These areas should be cleaned and disinfected after use by suspected or confirmed ARD patients. 16. HCWs should receive proper training on the use of PPE, including donning and doffing procedures, to ensure compliance and minimize contamination risks. 17. PPE supplies should be prioritized at the national and institutional levels, and the reuse of disposable PPE should be avoided unless absolutely necessary and performed under safe conditions. 18. If a patient’s body is removed from an isolation area, PPE should be used to avoid direct contact with body fluids. Families wishing to view the body should be allowed to do so under Standard Precautions. 19. Post-mortem examinations should only be performed when necessary, in well-ventilated rooms, and with appropriate PPE to protect staff. The number of personnel involved should be minimized. 20. Autopsies should be conducted in rooms with adequate ventilation (≥12 air changes per hour). Measures should be taken to reduce aerosol generation, such as avoiding power saws and using exhaust ventilation systems. 21. Medical masks should fit tightly and be discarded immediately after use. If a mask becomes wet or soiled, it must be replaced promptly. 22. Gloves should be reserved for situations involving contact with blood, respiratory secretions, or body fluids, especially during aerosol-generating procedures. If supplies are limited, gowns may be reused in cohort areas under strict conditions. 23. Eye protection, such as goggles or face shields, should be used instead of conventional eyeglasses, which do not provide adequate protection against splashes. Eye protection must be cleaned and disinfected properly after each use. 24. PPE is intended to protect the user but should not increase risks to others or the environment. Unnecessary use of PPE should be avoided, and reuse should only occur under safe conditions. 25. Embalming and other mortuary care procedures may be conducted following Standard Precautions and local regulations. Families should be informed of risks and provided with PPE if necessary. 26. Post-mortem examinations should be performed only when essential, with safety measures in place, and in well-ventilated rooms. Staff involved should wear appropriate PPE and follow strict protocols to minimize infection risks.
